This is a standalone primer on conformal prediction, written as shared background for this blog's posts on conformal language modeling, conformal factuality, and related calibration work.

## What conformal prediction is

Conformal prediction [[1]](#ref-1), [[2]](#ref-2) is a distribution-free statistical framework that turns any predictor into one that outputs *sets* with a calibrated coverage guarantee. Given a trained model and a labeled *calibration set* not used in training, score each calibration example with some non-conformity function (for example, $1 - p(y_i \mid x_i)$ for classification), take the $(1-\epsilon)$-quantile of those scores, and at test time return every candidate whose score falls below that quantile. If the calibration and test data are exchangeable, the returned set contains the true label with probability at least $1-\epsilon$, without assumptions about the model's own calibration or the data distribution. The framework dates to the late 1990s (Vovk, Gammerman, and Shafer) and is a standard tool for uncertainty quantification outside deep learning.

## A concrete CIFAR-10 walkthrough

Take a CIFAR-10 image classifier with softmax outputs and target $\epsilon = 0.1$. On 1,000 held-out calibration images, score each by $s_i = 1 - p(y_i \mid x_i)$ (one minus the model's probability on the true class). Sort the 1,000 scores in ascending order and take the 901st value (the $\lceil 0.9 \cdot 1001 \rceil$-th); call it $\hat{q}$. On a new test image $x$, return the set of classes $\{y : 1 - p(y \mid x) \leq \hat{q}\}$. When the test image comes from the same distribution as calibration, the returned *set* contains the correct class at least 90% of the time. This is a weaker claim than "the top-1 prediction is correct 90% of the time" — a set of all 10 classes trivially contains the truth yet carries no information. Depending on difficulty, the set might contain one class (easy image), three or four (moderate), or all ten (a hard image the model has no clear read on). The number of distinct classes in the set is how conformal prediction communicates uncertainty, widening on harder inputs.

## Two knobs control set size

At a given coverage level, two knobs determine how big the returned set ends up. Smaller $\epsilon$ demands tighter coverage, pushes the calibration quantile into the right tail, and forces $\hat{q}$ up, so more candidates pass the test-time filter. At the extreme $\epsilon < 1/(n+1)$, where $n$ is the calibration set size, the quantile is undefined and the set becomes "everything," which satisfies the guarantee trivially but carries no information.

Model quality is the second knob. A better predictor assigns higher probability to the true class on calibration points, giving smaller non-conformity scores, a lower $\hat{q}$, and a stricter probability floor at test time. Because a better model still puts enough mass on the correct class to clear that stricter floor, it produces sharper sets at the same $\epsilon$. Weaker models hit the same coverage but through larger, less informative sets. Set size then doubles as a data-driven measure of model quality pegged to a formal guarantee.

## Ranking drives the guarantee

One subtlety worth naming: conformal prediction uses score *rankings*, and the coverage guarantee does not require the model's probabilities to be calibrated. Any monotone-in-relevance scoring function works, because the quantile adapts to whatever the calibration scores look like. The cost of miscalibration shows up in set size rather than coverage: a rank-destroying miscalibration inflates $\hat{q}$ and dilates the set, but the $(1-\epsilon)$ guarantee still holds.

## The returned set is a coverage hull

This means the returned set is a coverage hull. It does not carry relative likelihoods across elements, calibrated per-candidate confidences, or any distributional information beyond "at least one of these is correct at the chosen $\epsilon$." If a downstream consumer needs to know which answer in the set is most likely, conformal prediction leaves that to a separate mechanism, whether a raw ranking used informally or a Bayesian or ensemble method layered on top.

## Why generative LMs are harder

The framework above assumes a finite candidate set you can enumerate (the $K$ classes). Generative language models break this assumption: the output space is the combinatorial space of all possible text sequences, so you can't score every candidate. Adapting conformal prediction to LMs requires replacing enumeration with sampling plus a calibrated stopping rule. That adaptation is the subject of the [Conformal Language Modeling](/posts/20260505-conformal-language-modeling/) post. A related adaptation, specifically for factual claim verification, is the subject of the [Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees](/posts/20260505-conformal-factuality/) post.
